IX.1.title: What he seldom spoke of
IX.1.reflection: The Master rarely spoke of profit, of fate and of ren. The last item is puzzling, since ren is everywhere in the book. One reading is that he rarely spoke of it in the abstract, only in answers to particular people; another reading of the grammar makes him rarely speak of profit, but approve of fate and ren.
IX.1.question: What do you value most that you rarely speak of directly?

IX.2.title: I will take up charioteering
IX.2.reflection: A villager says Confucius is great, broadly learned, but famous for nothing in particular. The Master jokes: what should I specialise in? Archery? Driving? I will take up driving. Driving was the humblest of the gentlemanly arts. He answers praise mixed with criticism with self-mockery.
IX.2.question: How do you answer praise that carries a hidden criticism?

IX.3.title: The cap and the bow
IX.3.reflection: The ritual cap should be of linen; now silk is used because it is cheaper, and Confucius follows the majority. Ritual requires bowing below the hall; now people bow only after ascending, which is presumptuous, and he keeps the old way against the majority. He changes where change is harmless and resists where it shows disrespect.
IX.3.question: Which customs have you let change, and which do you keep against the crowd?

IX.4.title: Four things he was free of
IX.4.reflection: He had no fixed preconceptions, no insistence on certainty, no stubbornness, no self-centredness. Four absences describe the Master as well as any list of virtues.
IX.4.question: Which of the four do you most need to be free of?

IX.5.title: Danger in Kuang
IX.5.reflection: Surrounded and threatened in Kuang, where he was mistaken for a man who had wronged the town, Confucius says: King Wen is dead, but is culture not here with me? If Heaven meant culture to perish, it would not have given it to me; if not, what can the people of Kuang do? Like VII.22, a moment of composure resting on a sense of what he carried.
IX.5.question: What are you carrying that matters more than your own safety?

IX.6.title: Many small skills
IX.6.reflection: An official asks Zigong whether the Master is a sage, he has so many skills. Zigong says Heaven made him nearly a sage and gave him many abilities. Confucius corrects them: he was poor when young, so he learned many humble skills. Does the junzi need many? Not many. He refuses to have his practical skills counted as wisdom.
IX.6.question: What skill did you learn only because you had to?

IX.7.title: Both ends of the question
IX.7.reflection: Do I have knowledge? No. But if a simple man asks me something, even if I am empty, I take up the question from both ends and exhaust it. His method is not a store of answers but a way of examining questions.
IX.7.question: What question are you facing that you have only looked at from one end?

IX.8.title: No phoenix, no chart
IX.8.reflection: The phoenix does not come, the river gives no chart: it is over for me. Both were omens of a sage ruler's appearance. Confucius despairs of living to see good government. It is a rare moment of personal hopelessness.
IX.8.question: What sign are you waiting for that has not come?

IX.9.title: Rising for the mourner
IX.9.reflection: When he saw someone in mourning, someone in official dress, or a blind person, he would rise even if they were young, and pass them with hurried steps. Respect is shown in the body.
IX.9.question: How does your body show respect, without words?

IX.10.title: The higher I look
IX.10.reflection: Yan Hui sighs: the more I look up, the higher it is; the more I bore into it, the harder; I see it before me and suddenly it is behind. The Master leads step by step, broadens me with culture and restrains me with ritual. I cannot stop, and when I have used all my strength, something stands sheer before me, and I find no way to follow. It is the most moving account of a student's experience in the book.
IX.10.question: What have you pursued that always seemed to stay just ahead?

IX.11.title: Pretend ministers
IX.11.reflection: When the Master was very ill, Zilu had disciples act as his retainers, as if he still held office. Recovering, Confucius rebukes him: whom would I deceive? Heaven? Better to die in the arms of you, my disciples, than among retainers. Even if I have no grand burial, will I die by the roadside? He wants the truth of his situation honoured, not a fiction.
IX.11.question: Where have you kept up an appearance that deceives no one?

IX.12.title: A precious jade
IX.12.reflection: Zigong asks: if there were a beautiful jade, should one hide it in a box or sell it for a good price? Sell it, sell it, Confucius says; I am waiting for a buyer. The jade is the Master himself, waiting for a ruler who would employ him.
IX.12.question: What gift of yours are you keeping in a box?

IX.13.title: Among the Nine Tribes
IX.13.reflection: Confucius wants to go and live among the eastern tribes. Someone objects that they are uncouth. If a junzi lived among them, what uncouthness would there be? The answer combines the cultural confidence of his time with a belief that conduct transforms a place.
IX.13.question: What place would you change by living in it well?

IX.14.title: The music set right
IX.14.reflection: After returning from Wei to Lu, Confucius put the music in order, and the court songs and hymns each found their proper place. It is one of the few concrete achievements the book credits to him.
IX.14.question: What have you put back in order that had drifted?

IX.15.title: What I can manage
IX.15.reflection: To serve high officials abroad and father and elder brothers at home, to give all one can to funerals, and not to be troubled by wine: what difficulty do I have with these? Legge reads the end as "which of these do I attain to?", a modest question. Others read it as a quiet claim that these are within his reach.
IX.15.question: What ordinary duties are you sure you manage, and are you right?

IX.16.title: By the river
IX.16.reflection: Standing by a river, the Master says: it passes on like this, never ceasing, day and night. The line has been read as grief at time passing and as praise of steady effort. Both readings are old.
IX.16.question: What, in your life, keeps passing on like the river?
IX.16.exercise: Stand for a minute by moving water, or watch rain, and think of one thing that has been flowing through your days.

IX.17.title: Virtue and beauty
IX.17.reflection: I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. The sentence repeats in XV.13. The comparison is with an attraction that needs no effort at all.
IX.17.question: What good do you love as easily as a beautiful face?

IX.18.title: One basket of earth
IX.18.reflection: Learning is like raising a mound: if one basket short I stop, it is I who stop. It is like levelling ground: if I add one basket, it is I who advance. Progress and failure are both one's own, one basket at a time.
IX.18.question: What one basket of earth would you add today?
IX.18.exercise: Do one small piece of a task you have stopped, just one basket's worth.

IX.19.title: Never tired
IX.19.reflection: The one who never grew tired when I spoke to him: that was Hui. A short memory of a student's attention.
IX.19.question: When do you listen without growing tired?

IX.20.title: I never saw him stop
IX.20.reflection: Of Yan Hui, after his death: alas, I saw him advance, I never saw him stop. Grief and praise in one breath.
IX.20.question: What would you want said of you, that someone saw you advance?

IX.21.title: Sprouting without flower
IX.21.reflection: There are sprouts that never flower and flowers that never fruit. The image is often taken as a lament for Yan Hui, dead before his promise was fulfilled. It speaks of any promise that does not ripen.
IX.21.question: What promise in you has sprouted but not yet flowered?

IX.22.title: Respect the young
IX.22.reflection: The young should be held in awe: how do we know they will not equal us? But if at forty or fifty nothing is heard of them, they need not be feared. Respect for the future is joined to a frank deadline.
IX.22.question: Whom younger than you might surpass you, and how do you treat them?

IX.23.title: Agreeing is not enough
IX.23.reflection: Who can fail to agree with a stern correction? What matters is to change. Who can fail to be pleased by gentle advice? What matters is to think it through. Someone who is pleased but does not reflect, who agrees but does not change: I can do nothing with them.
IX.23.question: What advice have you agreed with and not acted on?

IX.24.title: First principles, again
IX.24.reflection: The second half of I.8 returns in the same words: hold to good faith, befriend no one not your equal, do not be afraid to correct your faults. Another repeated saying, perhaps from a different notebook.
IX.24.question: Since you first read this in Book I, have you corrected anything?

IX.25.title: The will of a common man
IX.25.reflection: An army can be robbed of its commander; a common man cannot be robbed of his will. The chapter puts the inner resolve of an ordinary person above military power.
IX.25.question: What in you could no one take away?

IX.26.title: In a shabby robe
IX.26.reflection: Dressed in a worn padded robe, standing beside men in furs, and not ashamed: that is Zilu. The Master quotes an ode: not envious, not greedy, how could he not be good? Zilu keeps repeating the lines, and Confucius says: that is not enough to be good. Praise, and then a check on pride in the praise.
IX.26.question: What praise have you repeated to yourself a little too often?

IX.27.title: Pine and cypress
IX.27.reflection: Only when the year turns cold do we know that the pine and cypress are the last to fade. Character shows in hardship. It is one of the most painted images in Chinese art.
IX.27.question: Whose steadiness did you see only in a hard season?

IX.28.title: Not perplexed, not anxious, not afraid
IX.28.reflection: The wise are not perplexed, the humane not anxious, the brave not afraid. Three virtues, each freeing from one kind of trouble. XIV.28 repeats them, with Confucius saying he has none of the three.
IX.28.question: Which of the three troubles visits you most?

IX.29.title: How far we can go together
IX.29.reflection: Some can study with us but not go toward the Way; some can go toward the Way but not stand firm in it; some can stand firm but not weigh circumstances with us. Companions part at different stages. The last, weighing, is judgement in the particular case.
IX.29.question: With whom can you study, with whom stand firm, and with whom weigh a hard case?

IX.30.title: Not truly far
IX.30.reflection: A lost ode: the cherry blossoms flutter, how can I not think of you, but your house is far. Confucius comments: he does not really think of her, or how could it be far? Distance is a measure of desire. Many read the beloved as the Way.
IX.30.question: What do you call far away that you have simply not set out for?
